newsitem.title: UK: Several hurt by bombs at N.Ireland army base.
newsitem.headline: Several hurt by bombs at N.Ireland army base.

text.p: Up to 20 people were injured when two bombs exploded inside Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast, on Monday.
Police confirmed that the blasts, which could be heard 10 miles (16 km) away in Belfast, were caused by bombs.
There was speculation in the security forces that the explosions were caused by mortars, a favoured weapon of Irish Republican guerrilla groups fighting British rule in Northern Ireland.
Police said there were "multiple casualties" and hospitals were told to expect around 20 victims of the explosion, some with leg injuries and others with burns.
Army spokesmen said black smoke hung over the base.
Police said no bomb warning had been given by any of Northern Ireland's feuding guerrilla groups and there was no immediate claim of responsibility.
But spokesmen for the majority Protestant community, which wants the province to stay British, accused Irish Republican guerrilla groups of responsibility.
"This is obviously a Republican attack from whatever quarter," said Gary McMichael of the Ulster Democratic Party.
"Obviously it is a very serious incident and the ramifications could be quite considerable," said David Trimble of the Ulster Unionist Party, the biggest pro-British political group in the province.

"All we know at the moment is that there have been two bombs...and up to 20 casualties. The probablity is that this is the work of a Republican organisation and marks quite a significant development in the renewed Republican campaign," Trimble told BBC radio.
It was not known whether soldiers were injured in the attack. The precise number of troops at the base is secret.

Northern Ireland has been largely immune from violence since rival guerrilla groups called ceasefires in 1994, but the Irish Republican Army (IRA) went back to war against British rule with attacks on British mainland targets in February.
It has avoided targets in Northern Ireland for fear of provoking a backlash by Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas fighting to maintain British rule of the province, security sources believe.

Police chiefs say that any IRA attack in Northern Ireland itself would provoke retaliation by Loyalists, who could also target the Irish Republic, which they accuse of backing the IRA goal of reuniting the two Irelands.
Last week police found a car bomb packed with explosives in Belfast and a breakaway Irish Republican group claimed reponsibility for planting the device, which failed to detonate.
